title: Ashtpadi 16, salok: no form, no color
hook: roop na rekh na rang kichh: He has no form, no outline, no color (Sukhmani 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 15, taan, and your line: borrowed strength. Did you ask for strength before something hard? Today a new ashtpadi, the sixteenth, and a salok that seems to argue with this week. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

Two days ago, the picture was dye: everything soaked in His color. Today, the very next ashtpadi opens by saying He has no color at all. If you were reading closely, that might stop you. Which is it? Is God the dye that soaks every thread, or something with no color whatsoever? It can look like a contradiction. It's a pattern worth learning to spot, because Gurbani holds the two together on purpose. Today: no form, no color.
screen: `TWO DAYS AGO: IN HIS COLOR.` → `TODAY: NO COLOR AT ALL.` → `WHICH IS IT?`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: He has no form, no outline, no color at all; God is beyond the three qualities. Nanak, He makes Himself understood to the one with whom He is pleased. Three nos to start. Roop: form, shape, appearance. Rekh: a line, an outline, the edge you'd trace if you drew something. Rang: color. If you've been on this path since the start of the year, these may sound familiar. Jaap Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh's morning hymn, opened the same way: no mark, no sign, no color, no caste. And the short lines we met in Jaap's chachari meter: aroop hain, You are formless. Its opening verse even uses the salok's three words, roop, rang and rekh. So Guru Arjan and Guru Gobind Singh describe the One in the same breath of negatives. Now the puzzle. How can God have no color and also be the color everything happens in? Take light. White light has no color of its own; you can't point to it in a rainbow. And yet every color you see is that light, split and shining. Or water: no shape of its own, and it takes the shape of every glass. Having no color of your own is exactly what lets you be in every color. Something with a fixed outline can only be in one place; something with no outline can be everywhere. Gurdwaras keep no images of God. In this picture, that isn't because God is far from shapes. It's that no single shape could hold the One. Next two days, the salok's other phrases: beyond the three qualities, and known by those He blesses.
screen: `ROOP, REKH, RANG: FORM, LINE, COLOR.` · `JAAP SAID IT TOO.` · `LIGHT HAS NO COLOR, AND IS ALL COLOR.` · `NO OUTLINE, SO EVERYWHERE.` · then, large: `NO FORM, NO COLOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: close your eyes and rest. Behind your eyelids, notice what's there: maybe a dim glow, drifting specks, a soft darkness. No shapes worth naming, no outlines, no real colors. Don't try to make a picture. Just rest in the not-picture. If an image of anything starts to form, let it fade. If you pray, you can hold the word Waheguru without picturing anything at all. The bell holds the time.
Rekh, a line, an outline. Roop na rekh na rang: no form, no outline, no color, and so able to be in every form and every color.
Your line: no form, no color. Today, catch one moment of light on a wall or a window, and remember it has no color of its own. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the sixteenth ashtpadi with the salok roop na rekh na rang kichh, and gurdwaras keep no images of God, since no single form could contain the Formless.

fork.setup: Sukhmani says everything happens in His color, then says He has no color. how can both be true?
options: one of them is a mistake.
having no color of your own lets you be in every color.
fork.reveal: like white light or water: no color or shape of its own, and so present in all of them.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rekh, a line or outline, the edge of a shape.

trapdoor: what you thought: formless means God is absent from the world of things.
what it means: with no outline of its own, the One isn't limited to any one place or form.
what a scholar hears: the salok's chain of negatives (roop na rekh na rang) belongs to a long Indian tradition of describing the ultimate by what it is not, also heard in Jaap Sahib's opening.

notes: Salok of ashtpadi 16 paraphrased: roop na rekh na rang kichh trihu gun te prabh bhinn; tiseh bujhaae Nanakaa jis hovai suprasann. Confirm Ang 283.
Jaap Sahib stanza 1 paraphrased as 'no mark, no sign, no color, no caste': confirm.
'A century apart' for Guru Arjan (Sukhmani, c. 1600) and Guru Gobind Singh (Jaap, late 1600s): approximate.
